title: The Retention Agreement: Why Your Key People Have to Sign Before a Buyer Will Pay Full Price
linkedin:
A signed term sheet doesn't always mean a settled price.

Partway through due diligence, a lot of buyers send through retention agreements for a handful of key staff, asking them to commit to staying twelve to eighteen months after settlement.

It looks administrative. It isn't.

A buyer isn't paying for last year's profit and loss statement. They're paying for the expectation that the cash flow behind it keeps showing up after they take over. If a meaningful share of revenue or client relationships sits with two or three people other than the owner, the buyer has no real way to verify that without a formal commitment from those people to stay.

The part most owners miss is where the cost of that commitment actually sits. In plenty of deals, retention isn't funded separately by the buyer. It's structured as a holdback against the purchase price, or folded into an earnout tied to the same people staying and performing. The number on the letter of intent was never fully yours to bank on day one.

Strip the legal language away and a retention agreement is really just owner dependence, priced in dollar terms, the same dependence that quietly discounts the multiple long before any term sheet exists.

The owners who move through this cleanly aren't negotiating retention terms for the first time in due diligence. They built the incentive structures and the career paths years earlier, so the agreement reads as confirmation, not a new demand under pressure.

Ever heard of a buyer asking your key staff to sign a "please stay" agreement before they'll settle on your business?

It happens more than people think. A buyer isn't just paying for last year's numbers, they're paying for the relationships and know-how that keep the business running after you've handed over the keys. If that mostly sits with two or three people, the buyer wants it in writing that they're staying, and sometimes holds back part of your price until they do.

Here's the real question though: if someone asked your best people to commit to eighteen more months today, would they sign without blinking?

A note for Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victorian business owners who are thinking about a sale sometime in the next few years.

When a sale moves into due diligence, a lot of buyers ask a handful of key staff, an operations manager, a senior tradesperson, a long-serving team lead, to sign a retention agreement committing them to stay for twelve to eighteen months after settlement. It can feel like a small administrative step. It usually isn't.

What the buyer is actually doing is pricing how much of the business's future cash flow depends on people other than the owner. In a lot of deals, the cost of that retention isn't paid separately. It's held back from the purchase price, or built into an earnout, which means the figure on the letter of intent is not always the figure that ends up in the bank.

The businesses that handle this cleanly are usually the ones that built genuine career paths and incentive structures for their key people years before a buyer ever appeared, so the eventual agreement confirms an existing relationship rather than asking for something new under pressure.

If you're weighing up a sale down the track, it's worth understanding how dependent your business currently is on a handful of people, well before a buyer starts asking.
